newsitem.title: UK: Russia GKOs lose a little lustre with yield cut.
newsitem.headline: Russia GKOs lose a little lustre with yield cut.

text.p: Russia's cut on Tuesday of yields to foreigners of its Treasury bills (GKOs) inevitably removes some of their charm but analysts said they are still worth holding.
Russia cut GKO yields for non-resident investors to 13 percent from 16 percent from December 5, but also lowered the minimum term to repatriate the proceeds to two months from one month.
"It is still not a bad rate of return. Where else can you put money and get that type of return?" said Deutsche Morgan Grenfell local currency analyst David Atkinson.
Six-month GKOs currently yield 38 percent for local buyers.
"We were all expecting them to lower yields but three percent is a bit more than expected," said Mark Fisher, who heads local currency trading in emerging markets at ING Barings.
"I wouldn't want to see it (the yield) come down much more," he added.
Foreigners officially may only repatriate the funds through forward currency deals or options.

"The shift to two months is positive," said Merrill Lynch senior emerging markets analyst Dan McGovern, though he added the cut in yields were a sign Russian authorities were trying to make GKOs a little less attractive.
However, with annualised hedged returns of 23-24 percent for six-month bills, meant GKOs were still attractive.
Analaysts said Tuesday's announcement of an extension of the rouble corridor, allowing a gentle depreciation next year, was good news by providing a stable currency environment.
However, a Russian debt trader at one bank said the changes would dim the market's allure.
"Investors will think twice about getting into the T-bill market. Opportunities are really flattening out," he said, pointing to alternatives such as MinFin bonds.
